classification_profile.title: Stanford University Risk Classifications (Low / Moderate / High)
classification_profile.description:
The three risk-based classifications published by Stanford University IT, together with the Minimum Security Standards stated per classification for endpoints, servers, and applications. Two living web pages, read as retrieved: neither carries a version or an effective date, which is why every citation here is dated by retrieval rather than by publication.

Paired with the UC profile deliberately. Three word-named levels against four ascending alphanumeric codes is the pairing that stresses the model hardest: any implementation that assumed four levels, or that derived order from a label, works on one of these two and silently fails on the other.

An EXAMPLE, not a maintained document. Fork it, correct automat's reading against your own reading, and re-attest.

interpretation.attribution: Risk Classifications and Minimum Security Standards, published by Stanford University IT (Information Security Office) at uit.stanford.edu. Quoted and closely read here for interoperability; the published pages are the authoritative text and are revised in place without a version bump — the hashes in sources[] are the only fixed reference to what was read.
interpretation.non_endorsement: This is automat's interpretation of a published policy. It was not authored, reviewed, or endorsed by Stanford University. The institution's own policy governs; verify against it.

signatures.statement: We read the two cited published pages and wrote this profile as our own reading of them. This attests to authorship of the reading and to nothing else: not that the reading is correct, not that it is complete, and not that Stanford University has seen it. Both sources are living pages that may have changed since the retrieval timestamps recorded here. No signature material accompanies this attestation, and automat verifies none in v1. Re-attested at AUDIT-2 (F7), when every control and external-obligation citation was corrected to name both cells it is read from — the "What to do" cell holding the requirement text and the risk cell holding applicability at this level — having previously named only the risk cell, which holds a two-word applicability marker rather than the text being transcribed. Re-attested rather than re-hashed: this attests that we read the cited cells, and the correction changed which cells are cited. The table structure was re-read at the source URI before the citations were changed; no requirement text was altered. The same re-attestation covers F8: determination.roles[] now says in its own text that "Data owner" is automat's inference rather than a role the source designates, the source naming no determination authority at all.

roles: Data owner (automat's inference, not a role the source designates — see determination.process)
determination.process:
Review the classification definitions and the published example tables, and select the highest applicable risk designation across all of them. The Minimum Security Standards state the rule per asset class in the same words each time: determine the risk level by reviewing the data, server, and application risk classification examples and selecting the highest applicable risk designation across all — so an endpoint storing Low Risk data but used to access a High Risk application is designated High Risk. For High Risk servers and applications the standards add a security, privacy, and legal review: follow the institution's data risk assessment process and implement its recommendations prior to deployment.

The source names NO determination authority at all, and "Data owner" in roles[] is automat's inference rather than the source's designation — which is why that entry says so in its own text (AUDIT-2 F8). The phrase appears in the Risk Classifications page exactly twice, both times as a parenthetical qualifying an example row: "Research data (at data owner's discretion)" under Low Risk and "Unpublished research data (at data owner's discretion)" under Moderate Risk. Discretion over two example rows is not the same claim as authority over a determination, and the schema's roles[] has minItems 1, so this profile cannot express "the source designates nobody" by leaving the list empty — it expresses it in the value instead. The inference is a reasonable one and it is still an inference: an operator who needs to know whose determination they are recording should ask their own institution rather than rely on this field. Where a classification is unclear, the pages direct questions to the Information Security Office and the University Privacy Office; those are contacts the source names for questions, not roles it makes responsible for determining a level, and they are deliberately not listed as determination roles here.

Go and ask the data owner. There is no step in this process that a tool performs.

citation.section: Minimum Security Standards: Endpoints, introductory paragraph
citation.quote: Determine the risk level by reviewing the data risk classification examples, server risk classification examples, and application risk classification examples and selecting the highest applicable risk designation across all. For example, an endpoint storing Low Risk Data but utilized to access a High Risk application is designated as High Risk.

determination.notes:
Neither published page addresses whether a determiner may classify above or below the level the examples indicate, and the record shows that asymmetrically on purpose. may_raise carries the explicit value not-stated, which records that automat looked and the source was silent. may_lower is ABSENT rather than carrying an equivalent value: its vocabulary has no not-stated member, because the block exists to describe a route the source names, and an absent block is the unambiguous way to say there is none.

The contrast with the UC profile is the whole reason both are shipped. UC states the raise and lower rules explicitly and asymmetrically, naming an exception process for lowering. Any consumer that read a missing may_lower as permission would be wrong in the permissive direction on this profile and correct on the other, which is the hardest kind of defect to notice.

levels.label: Low Risk
levels.definition: Data and systems are classified as Low Risk if they are not considered to be Moderate or High Risk, and: the data is intended for public disclosure, or the loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the data or system would have no adverse impact on our mission, safety, finances, or reputation.

citation.section: Risk Classifications, Low Risk definition
citation.quote: Data and systems are classified as Low Risk if they are not considered to be Moderate or High Risk, and: The data is intended for public disclosure, or The loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the data or system would have no adverse impact on our mission, safety, finances, or reputation.

examples: Information authorized to be available on or through the university's website without authentication
Policy and procedure manuals designated by the owner as public
University contact information not designated by the individual as "private"
levels.notes: The definition is residual — Low Risk is what is left after Moderate and High are ruled out — which is the source's own construction and is preserved rather than rewritten into a positive definition. Note the consequence for composition: a residual bottom level cannot be reached by elimination in a mixed dataset, because the highest-water-mark rule resolves the mixture upward first.

levels.label: Moderate Risk
levels.definition: Data and systems are classified as Moderate Risk if they are not considered to be High Risk, and: the data is not generally available to the public, or the loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the data or system could have a mildly adverse impact on our mission, safety, finances, or reputation.

citation.section: Risk Classifications, Moderate Risk definition
citation.quote: Data and systems are classified as Moderate Risk if they are not considered to be High Risk, and: The data is not generally available to the public, or The loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the data or system could have a mildly adverse impact on our mission, safety, finances, or reputation.

examples: Unpublished research data (at data owner's discretion)
Faculty and staff employment applications, personnel files, benefits, salary, birth date, personal contact information
Non-public university policies and policy manuals
University internal memos and email, non-public reports, budgets, plans, financial information
Engineering, design, and operational information regarding university infrastructure

levels.label: High Risk
levels.definition: Data and systems are classified as High Risk if: protection of the data is required by law or regulation, the university is required to self-report to the government and/or provide notice to the individual if the data is inappropriately accessed, or the loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the data or system could have a significant adverse impact on our mission, safety, finances, or reputation.

citation.section: Risk Classifications, High Risk definition
citation.quote: Data and systems are classified as High Risk if: Protection of the data is required by law/regulation, Stanford is required to self-report to the government and/or provide notice to the individual if the data is inappropriately accessed, or The loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the data or system could have a significant adverse impact on our mission, safety, finances, or reputation.

examples: Health information, including Protected Health Information (PHI)
Donor contact information and non-public gift information

external_obligations.name: PCI DSS

citation.section: Minimum Security Standards: Servers, Regulated Data Security Controls row — requirement text from the "What to do" cell, applicability from the High Risk cell
citation.quote: Implement PCI DSS, HIPAA, or export controls as applicable.

external_obligations.note: The source names the regime and says "as applicable" — it does not state that the regime applies. Whether it applies to this operator is the operator's declaration, which is why declared_by_operator is true and no obligation_profile_id is given: automat ships no PCI DSS obligation profile, and naming one that does not exist would be a claim about a document nobody has read.

citation.section: Minimum Security Standards: Servers, Regulated Data Security Controls row — requirement text from the "What to do" cell, applicability from the High Risk cell
citation.quote: Implement PCI DSS, HIPAA, or export controls as applicable.

external_obligations.name: FISMA

citation.section: Minimum Security Standards: Applications, Regulated Data Security Controls row — requirement text from the "What to do" cell, applicability from the High Risk cell
citation.quote: Implement PCI DSS, HIPAA, FISMA, or export controls as applicable.

external_obligations.note: Cited to the APPLICATIONS table specifically. FISMA appears in that table's regulated-data row and not in the endpoints or servers rows, and the difference is preserved rather than smoothed: a citation naming the servers table for a regime that table does not name would be unverifiable at the cell a reader turns to.

citation.section: Minimum Security Standards: Servers, Regulated Data Security Controls row — requirement text from the "What to do" cell, applicability from the High Risk cell
citation.quote: Implement PCI DSS, HIPAA, or export controls as applicable.

levels.notes: The published service table on the risk-classifications page states which classifications of data are permitted on which institutional services, including cloud infrastructure — and for cloud accounts it makes approval conditional on the provision being set up and managed by a named institutional team rather than on the classification alone. That table is not transcribed here, and its absence is not coverage: a per-service approval matrix changes far faster than a classification scheme, and a stale copy of it inside automat would tell an operator a service is approved for High Risk data when the institution has since said otherwise. Read it at the source.

The hash is over the HTML bytes as retrieved, not over extracted text — a hash whose input nobody can reproduce is decoration, and for a living page the hash is the only fixed reference to what was read.

No version and no date appear anywhere in the page, which is what date_basis retrieved-only records. sources.title: Minimum Security Standards — Stanford University IT
sources.note:
The hash is over the HTML bytes as retrieved.

THREE LIMITS ON WHAT MAY BE CLAIMED FROM THIS DOCUMENT.

First, scope. The page presents its standards under several tabs — endpoints, servers, applications, and further ones for infrastructure services, connected devices, and research — but only the endpoints, servers, and applications tables are present in the retrieved body; the remaining tabs are navigation with no content behind them at this URL. This profile therefore transcribes those three tables and claims NOTHING from the others. A level here is not a complete account of what the institution requires.

Second, transcription. Each row's "What to do" cell states an obligation and then names specific tools the institution recommends or provides for meeting it. The obligation is transcribed; the named tools are not. Two reasons, and the second is the load-bearing one: automat carries a standing rule against naming products or vendors other than AWS anywhere in its code, docs, or data, and a vendored catalog file is data automat ships. But independently of that rule, the source itself marks most of these as "recommended" — the requirement is encryption, not a particular disk-encryption product — so transcribing the tool as though it were the requirement would misstate the policy in the stricter direction. Where a tool is named without the word recommended, the requirement is transcribed generically ("require two-step authentication", "deploy host intrusion detection") and the institution's specific implementation is left at the source. Verify against the cited cell before relying on any control here; the citations name the exact row and cells so that comparison is a line-by-line one.

Third, which cell a control is read out of, because the table splits one claim across two. The risk columns hold only an applicability marker — "Required for Low Risk Data" and so on — while the requirement text itself is in the "What to do" cell, which is shared by every level the row applies to. So a control here is read from two cells: what to do from one, whether it applies at this level from the other. Every citation says so. Until AUDIT-2 (F7) they all named only the risk column, which is the cell that does NOT contain the text they were transcribing — a reader following the citation would have found a two-word marker where a requirement was claimed to be, and the correct text one cell to the left.
